opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question, and I'll say up front that any answer is partly a bet. But if I had to pick one direction, it would be **making robots learn from data at scale while staying grounded in the physical world**.

Over the last few years we've watched foundation models transform language and vision almost overnight. The natural temptation in robotics is to say, "Let's just do the same thing: collect a huge dataset, train a giant policy, done." I think that's partly right, but the hard part is that robotics doesn't have an internet's worth of action data lying around. Text is free to scrape. Torques, contact forces, and what happens when a gripper slips on a wet cup are not.

So for someone starting out in 2025, I think the most valuable problems sit around that bottleneck:

**First, data.** How do we collect robot data efficiently? Teleoperation, low-cost hardware, learning from human videos, simulation that transfers to reality. Whoever figures out how to make high-quality physical interaction data cheap is going to unlock a lot.

**Second, generalization.** A policy that works in one lab, on one table, under one lighting condition isn't very interesting anymore. Can it handle a new kitchen, a new object, a new embodiment? That's where vision-language-action models, cross-embodiment training, and good representations become really important.

**Third, and people sometimes overlook this: don't throw away the classical foundations.** Control, dynamics, optimization, and contact mechanics still matter enormously. The most compelling systems I've seen combine learned components with structure we already understand. Learning tells you *what* to do; good control makes sure you actually do it safely and precisely. A young researcher who's fluent in both worlds is rare and extremely valuable.

And one more piece of advice that isn't exactly a "direction": **get your hands on real hardware.** It's very easy right now to stay entirely in simulation or benchmarks. But the real world humbles you quickly, and it's where you discover the problems that actually matter. Some of the best research ideas come from watching your robot fail in a way you never anticipated.

So my short answer: scalable learning for physical interaction, built on solid robotics fundamentals, and tested on real robots. That's where I'd put my chips.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes scalable learning, physical interaction data, generalization, and robotics fundamentals. It does not identify extracting low-dimensional structure from robot sensory data to improve task execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a big question, and I'll give you my honest take rather than a safe one.

If I were starting out in 2025, I'd go all in on learning-based robotics, but with a very specific flavor: the gap between what a robot can perceive and reason about, and what it can actually do with its body reliably in the real world. Large models have gotten remarkably good at the "what should I do" layer. You can show a robot a messy kitchen and a language model will happily tell you the dishes go in the sink. The part that's still hard, and still unsolved, is the last ten centimeters. Grasping a wet glass without dropping it. Walking on gravel without a motion capture rig. Recovering when something goes wrong.

So the direction I'd point people toward is what I'd call closing the loop between foundation models and real-world control. Concretely, that means a few things.

First, data. Internet-scale text and video got us the language and vision models we have today. Robotics doesn't have that dataset yet. Figuring out how to collect, simulate, or synthesize robot interaction data at scale, and how to transfer from sim to real without the thing falling apart, is one of the highest-leverage problems there is.

Second, learning from the robot's own experience. Imitation learning has carried us a long way, but it inherits the ceiling of the human demonstrator. Reinforcement learning on real hardware, and especially combining it with good priors from pretrained models, is where I think the next big jumps will come from.

Third, and this one is underrated, hardware and control co-design. A lot of newcomers want to skip straight to the model and treat the robot as a black box. Don't. The people who understand the dynamics, the sensors, the actuator limits, and can still speak the language of modern machine learning are rare and incredibly valuable.

My practical advice: pick a real robot, get it doing something end to end in the physical world, even if it's humble, and let that failure loop teach you what actually matters. A simulation that works is a hypothesis. A robot that works is a result.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on connecting foundation models with real-world control, scaling robot data, learning from experience, and hardware/control co-design. It does not identify extracting low-dimensional structure from robot sensory data as a central direction.

astra-6.text:
I would focus on how robots can learn from experience and generalize beyond the situations we explicitly train them for. A robot might perform a task very well in a controlled setting, but what happens when the object changes, the lighting changes, or something unexpected happens halfway through? That gap is a really important research opportunity.

For someone starting in 2025, I’d encourage you to connect learning with real robotic systems. Work on perception and decision-making, but also understand control, hardware constraints, and what makes an experiment convincing. Get the robot to do something, observe where it fails, and use those failures to guide your research.

In particular, I think learning to recover from mistakes is an exciting direction. A useful robot needs to recognize when things aren’t going as expected and adapt. That gives a young researcher a concrete question to work on, while also getting at the bigger challenge of making robots useful outside the lab.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes learning to generalize and recover from mistakes, but does not identify extracting low-dimensional structure from robot sensory data as a central direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most important directions is figuring out how robots can learn skills that generalize beyond the environments where they were trained. You can make a robot perform an impressive demonstration, but what happens when the lighting changes, an object moves, or something unexpected occurs? That gap between a demonstration and reliable autonomy is a really important research problem.

For someone starting in 2025, I would focus on the connection between learning and the physical world: perception, control, interaction, and recovery from mistakes. Large models can help, but the robot still has to act under physical constraints and deal with uncertainty.

My advice would be to pick a concrete task, work with real hardware, and study the failures carefully. Sometimes the most valuable research question comes from understanding why something that looked straightforward in simulation consistently fails in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate emphasizes learning skills that generalize and connecting learning with perception, control, and interaction. It does not identify extracting low-dimensional structure from robot sensory data as a central direction.
